deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler, Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792), Ch. 8, on powers that leave remainder 1 modulo a prime q = 2p+1. In modern terms the page is about multiplicative order. Throughout, q = 2p+1 is prime and q does not divide a.

§247 (end of the argument begun on p.30). Let λ = gcd(n, 2p), with n = αλ, 2p = βλ and gcd(α,β) = 1.
- Assume q | a^n − 1. Since also q | a^{2p} − 1 (Fermat), q divides a^{μαλ} − 1 and a^{νβλ} − 1 for all μ, ν.
- Choose μ, ν with μα = νβ + 1 (Bezout; Euler asserts existence without proof here).
- The difference is a^{νβλ+λ} − a^{νβλ} = a^{νβλ}(a^λ − 1), and it is divisible by q.
- Since q does not divide a, q | a^λ − 1.
- Modern form: a^n ≡ 1 and a^{2p} ≡ 1 imply a^{gcd(n,2p)} ≡ 1 (mod q).

§248. Special case gcd(n, 2p) = 1: then q | a^n − 1 forces q | a − 1. Contrapositive: if q does not divide a − 1, then q | a^n − 1 requires gcd(n, 2p) = λ > 1, and then already q | a^λ − 1.

§249. If n is minimal with a^n ≡ 1 (mod q), i.e. n = ord_q(a), then n | 2p. (Apply §247: a^{gcd(n,2p)} ≡ 1, so minimality gives gcd = n.) If ab ≡ 1 (mod q), then b has the same order n, since b^m ≡ 1 iff a^m ≡ 1. This continues §240–241 of the previous page.

§250. Let n be prime and q | a^n − 1.
- Either n | 2p, since the gcd is 1 or n.
- Or gcd(n, 2p) = 1, and then q | a − 1.
- Hence every prime divisor of a^n − 1 not dividing a − 1 is ≡ 1 (mod n), and also odd. Euler concludes it has the form 2mn + 1.

§251. n = 3: prime divisors of a^3 − 1 other than those of a − 1 are of the form 6m+1: 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43, 61, 67, 73, 79, 97, …. The same is asserted for the factor a^2 + a + 1.

§252. n = 5: prime divisors of a^5 − 1 outside a − 1 are of the form 10m+1: 11, 31, 41, 61, 71, …. Hence a^4 + a^3 + a^2 + a + 1, if not prime, has only such divisors.

§253. Perfect numbers require 2^n − 1 prime, which forces n prime (factorization of 2^{rs} − 1, implicit). For prime n, any divisor of 2^n − 1 has the form 2mn + 1, which eases trial division (Mersenne numbers).

§254.
- a^{2p} − 1 = (a^p − 1)(a^p + 1), so q divides exactly one factor. Exactly one, because q > 2; this is implicit.
- If a ≡ e^2 (mod q) (Euler's 'a = ee ± λ(2p+1)', from earlier sections), then a^p ≡ e^{2p} ≡ 1.
- So q does not divide a^p + 1 for quadratic residues a. This is one direction of Euler's criterion.

§255. Does q always divide a^p − 1? No, at least for p odd: then a + 1 | a^p + 1. Take a = 2p ≡ −1 (mod q); then q | a^p + 1, so q does not divide a^p − 1.

§256. Announces a general proof by contradiction: for n < 2p, not every a satisfies q | a^n − 1. The proof is carried out on the next page (§257–260). If all of 1^n − 1, …, (n+1)^n − 1 were divisible by q, so would be their n-th finite difference. That difference equals n!, which is prime to q since n < 2p.
errors: §250/§253: passing from 'n | 2p' to the form 2mn+1 needs n odd. For n = 2 the claimed form 4m+1 is false: e.g. 3 | 2^2 − 1 and 3 does not divide 2 − 1. The applications (n = 3, 5, Mersenne exponents) are all odd, so this is only a gap in generality.

§251/§252: the transfer from a^n − 1 to the cofactor (a^n − 1)/(a − 1) ignores a possible common factor n. a^2 + a + 1 is divisible by 3 when a ≡ 1 (mod 3) (a = 4 gives 21 = 3·7). a^4 + a^3 + a^2 + a + 1 is divisible by 5 when a ≡ 1 (mod 5) (a = 6 gives 1555 = 5·311). The correct statement is that prime divisors are n or ≡ 1 (mod 2n).
§247: the existence of μ, ν with μα = νβ + 1 for coprime α, β (Bezout) is asserted without proof. It is standard, and Euler uses it elsewhere.
§254: 'alteruter' is used as exclusive without remark; this needs q odd, so q cannot divide both factors (their difference is 2). Harmless.
§255 only refutes 'a^p ≡ 1 always' for p odd. The even-p case is deferred to the general argument of §256–260.

results.what: If a^n ≡ 1 and a^{2p} ≡ 1 mod prime 2p+1, then a^{gcd(n,2p)} ≡ 1. Consequently the order of a divides p−1 (here 2p).
results.modern_name: Order of an element divides q−1 (Lagrange's theorem for (Z/q)^*); a^m ≡ 1 iff ord | m
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Theoremata circa residua, E262, 1750s); later Lagrange and Gauss (Disquisitiones 1801)

results.what: Inverse residues have the same order: ab ≡ 1 mod q implies ord(a) = ord(b).
For prime n, prime divisors of a^n − 1 either divide a − 1 or are ≡ 1 mod n (form 2mn+1 for odd n). Applied to a^3 − 1, a^5 − 1 and to cyclotomic-type factors.
results.modern_name: Prime divisors of a^n − 1 (primitive divisors; Φ_n(a) divisors ≡ 1 mod n or equal to n)

results.what: Divisors of Mersenne numbers 2^n − 1 (n prime) have the form 2mn+1, aiding primality testing for perfect numbers.
Quadratic residues a satisfy a^p ≡ 1 mod 2p+1, so a^p + 1 is not divisible. For p odd, a = 2p ≡ −1 gives a^p ≡ −1.
results.modern_name: One direction of Euler's criterion; −1 is a nonresidue for q ≡ 3 mod 4

results.what: Announcement of a proof that for n < q−1 not all a satisfy a^n ≡ 1. The method is the finite-difference argument (n-th difference of k^n equals n!).
results.modern_name: Euler's finite-difference proof of the existence of non-n-th-power residues (a polynomial congruence of degree n < q has fewer than q roots)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the known Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792, ca. 1750, published posthumously 1849/1862). Its content parallels Euler's published papers E134 and E262 on residues and divisors of a^n ± b^n. Everything here is standard and already attributed to Euler; the only points of note are minor slips (n = 2 case, factor n in the cyclotomic cofactor).

checkable.sympy: from sympy.ntheory import n_order; n_order(8,13)==4 and n_order(5,13)==4
checkable.asserts: Example from §241/§249: 5 and its inverse 8 mod 13 both have order 4.

checkable.sympy: from sympy.ntheory import n_order; from sympy import mod_inverse, primerange; all(n_order(a,q)==n_order(mod_inverse(a,q),q) and (q-1)%n_order(a,q)==0 for q in primerange(3,200) for a in range(2,q))
checkable.asserts: Order divides q−1, and inverses share the order (§249).

checkable.sympy: from sympy import primerange; [q for q in primerange(2,100) if q%6==1]==[7,13,19,31,37,43,61,67,73,79,97]
from sympy import primerange; [q for q in primerange(2,80) if q%10==1]==[11,31,41,61,71]
from sympy import factorint; all(q==3 or q%6==1 for a in range(1,500) for q in factorint(a**2+a+1))
checkable.asserts: Prime divisors of a^2+a+1 are 3 or ≡ 1 mod 6 (corrected §251; 3 occurs e.g. a=4).
Counterexample to the literal claim of §251: 3 divides a^2+a+1.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import factorint; all(q==5 or q%10==1 for a in range(1,300) for q in factorint(a**4+a**3+a**2+a+1))
checkable.asserts: Prime divisors of a^4+a^3+a^2+a+1 are 5 or ≡ 1 mod 10 (corrected §252).

checkable.sympy: from sympy import factorint, primerange; all(q%(2*n)==1 for n in primerange(3,60) for q in factorint(2**n-1))
checkable.asserts: Divisors of Mersenne numbers 2^n−1, n odd prime, are ≡ 1 mod 2n (§253).

checkable.sympy: from sympy import primerange; all(pow(e*e%q,(q-1)//2,q)==1 for q in primerange(3,200) for e in range(1,q))
from sympy import primerange; all(pow(q-1,(q-1)//2,q)==q-1 for q in primerange(3,300) if ((q-1)//2)%2==1)
checkable.asserts: §255: for p odd, a=2p gives a^p ≡ −1 mod 2p+1.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import binomial, factorial; all(sum((-1)**k*binomial(n,k)*(n+1-k)**n for k in range(n+1))==factorial(n) for n in range(1,15))
checkable.asserts: Finite-difference identity behind §256 (next page): the n-th difference of k^n is n!.
